stem: A 'less-than' ogive for a distribution is drawn by plotting cumulative frequencies against the upper class boundaries. For a frequency distribution with classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30, 30-40, and 40-50 having frequencies 5, 12, 18, 10, and 5 respectively, what is the cumulative frequency plotted against the upper boundary of the class 20-30?

per_option_rationale.rationale: 18 is just the frequency of the class 20-30, not the cumulative frequency up to its upper boundary; the student confused individual frequency with cumulative frequency.
30 results from adding only the first two class frequencies (5 + 12 = 17) incorrectly as 18 + 12 = 30, an arithmetic slip in the cumulation.
Cumulative frequency up to upper boundary 30 = 5 + 12 + 18 = 35. This is the less-than cumulative frequency for the class 20-30.
17 results from adding only the first two classes (5 + 12 = 17), stopping one class too early and missing the current class frequency of 18.

explanation: For a less-than ogive, each point represents the total count of observations below the upper class boundary. Up to boundary 30, we sum all frequencies in classes ending at or before 30: 5 + 12 + 18 = 35.

explanation_sections.punchline: The cumulative frequency at any upper boundary is the running total of ALL class frequencies from the start up to and including that class - not just the class's own frequency.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: less-than ogive uses cumulative frequencies at upper class boundaries. Map the givens: classes 0-10 (f=5), 10-20 (f=12), 20-30 (f=18). Cumulative at upper boundary 30 = 5 + 12 + 18 = 35.
explanation_sections.lesson: A less-than ogive always uses running totals; the cumulative frequency at any boundary includes every class up to and including that class.
explanation_sections.timing: 40 seconds. The trap is reading off just the class frequency (18) instead of the running cumulative sum. Eliminate option 1 (= individual frequency) and option 4 (= stops one class short) first.
